title: Our Favorite Brain-Boosting Toys for Kids of All Ages
author: @wired
content:
By testing kids’ physical and mental limits, these toys help children learn where the boundaries of their knowledge lie, and how to transcend them. Take a look at some of our favorite ways to color outside the lines.

Orbita MIDI Color Sequencer

This spinning sequencer is like musical roulette for budding ravers. Place the colored magnets anywhere on the four gray concentric rings, each of which controls a MIDI loop. Then plug the sequencer into a smartphone or computer, connect your favorite music software, and get creative. All four loops run simultaneously, with each magnet representing a different note or sound. You can adjust the pitch and mute individual loops too. Refreshingly mechanical, the Orbita makes visualizing music production child’s play. $458, playtronica.com

Lego Smart Play System Pokémon Sets

By combining a new smart brick with programmable NFC tags and minifigures, kids of all ages can now design and interact with Lego creations like never before. The 2- by 4-stud rechargeable smart brick is packed with a synthesizer, speaker, accelerometer, gyroscope, light and sound sensors, and LEDs. A positioning system can sense orientation between multiple smart bricks. A big bonus: Lego’s Smart Play System works entirely without attention-sucking screens.

Lego’s first Pokémon collab almost crashed the website, so surely the Danes had IT on standby when 12 new Smart Play kits came online. There are two all-in-one kits: Pikachu’s 400-piece Training House and the 751-piece Charizard-Jolteon battle, which include rechargeable smart bricks and NFC tags that can trigger lights, sounds, motion and sensing.

Already got some Smart Play? The 10 other compatible kits, including Mewtwo's Lab Break and Cubone and Gengar's Spooky Showdown, have the tags but not the Smart Bricks. $70 and up, lego.com

Stapelstein Rainbow Set

Interactive adventure play done with style, the Rainbow kit features six stacking stools, a balance board, plus a host of nesting pieces that can combine to be whatever their imagination demands. Stepping-stones, wobble course, color-sorting game, toddler throne, snack tray, spinner, fort barricades or floor-is-lava upgrade. The lightweight toxin-free, 100 percent recyclable EPP pieces are waterproof, wipe clean and strong enough for adults (396 pounds limit), so don’t forget to include grandma. $299, stapelstein.com

KidzLane Electronic Dance Mat

We can’t promise it will turn Jnr. into Fred Astaire overnight, but this impossibly good value dance mat will get your kids moving and (hopefully) tuckered out. Suitable for ages 6 to 12, it features a built-in speaker, Bluetooth and AUX so you can connect your own favorite songs, four built-in games with five difficulty levels, including a great “Simon Says” mode that gets them thinking as well as boogying. And before you ask, yes, the volume is adjustable, and batteries removable. $19, walmart.com

Takway Sweekar

Oh good, it’s a reimagined Tamagotchi, but instead of a few beepy-bleeps and button presses to keep it alive, Sweekar has loaded it with generative AI and given it a long-term memory, evolving dialog and “personality.” We’re sure it’ll be fine, and neglect won’t result in a lawsuit when the Robots finally take over, but for now we suggest erring on the side of caution and make sure the kids care for it carefully through Egg, Baby, Teen, and Adult stages. The 89-gram pocket pet also simulates body warmth and breathing, which isn’t creepy at all. $149, takway.ai

Looi Robot

LOOI turns your smartphone into a chirpy little tank-like desk robot, using the screen as its face and the camera, mic and processor as its brain. Snap on your phone (minimum iOS 17+, or Android 12+), open the app and, powered by ChatGPT, it can chat, remember preferences, react to touch and gestures, play motion games, avoid desk edges and make funny faces. It also doubles as a 10-watt wireless charger and adjustable phone stand, which makes it marginally more helpful than your last assistant—although it can’t, as yet, make the coffee. $239, looirobot.com

Crocs Super Mario Core Classic Clog

As hyped as a Supreme x Louis Vuitton collaboration, just a whole lot more fun, the Crocs Mushroom Kingdom takeover is a joyous celebration of polyethylene vinyl acetate footwear. The Core Classic Clog, available in adult and kids’ sizes features a detailed graphic print with classic in-game items like coins, Super Stars, and Green Shells, while the sole is wrapped in dimensional detailing resembling the green pipes and grassy terrain. And, naturally, each pair comes with Super Mushroom outer rivets, a “?” Block badge on the backstrap, and eight Jibbitz charms featuring Mario and Luigi. $70, crocs.com

Gibson x Loog Les Paul

Loog has been making fine learn-to-play guitars for more than 10 years, and its intuitive three-string axes make it easier for anyone to learn the basics before transitioning up to a full fretboard. After a successful partnership with Fender, they’ve now teamed up with Gibson to produce a mini electric guitar in either classic SG—putting the young in AC-DC’s Angus Young’s favorite axe—or with the iconic Les Paul curves shown here. And before you ask, these are proper instruments, with a solid poplar body, Canadian neck, rosewood fingerboard, single coil pick-up and 19 finger-friendly 1.8 mm frets. $229, loogguitars.com

Woom Wow Balance Bike

The perfect buy if your bambino has nailed the art of sitting and standing independently, and you want more chaotic fun and adventure in your life. This self-centering, self-balancing bike is designed for kids as young as 9 months (from 28 to 40 inches in height). It gives them a chance to become the next big name on Red Bull’s MotoGP roster before they’ve even realized that broccoli isn’t actually fun little trees. $199, woom.com

Kibu Headphones

Turn kids’ headphones into a brilliant STEM project, with snap-together parts they build before they listen. Kibu's wired cans are 3D printed from recycled and plant-based materials, use a standard 3.5-mm jack, limit volume to 85 dB, and have a second aux port for daisy-chaining with friends. Every part can be customized, repaired, replaced and eventually recycled, an attention to detail far too rare in adult, let alone kid’s tech. WIRED wishes more grown-up gear followed the same sustainable approach, with gear designed to be understood, and to last. $73, kibu.family

Marvin’s Miniblocks

By selling 35 million copies for the Gameboy alone, Tetris proved that a handful of simple shapes could become one of gaming’s most enduring obsessions. Marvin’s Miniblocks gives that idea a preschool-friendly, screen-free reboot with a wooden board, 42 chunky shapes and 10 pattern cards for building, matching, rotating and inventing. It is part puzzle, part construction set, and made from eco-friendly wood with non-toxic paint. There is one important detail missing though. $55, the-littlemarvin.com

HoverAir Aqua

This 34 mph follow-me drone has 10 flight modes, 4K, 100 FPS motion camera and floating waterproof housing making it also the first design capable of take of and landing on water. It weighs under 250 grams, meaning you wont need FAA registration to fly one. The battery has enough for 23 minutes of flying time, and there's 128 GB built-in storage. Plus, with a level 7 wind resistance, it’s happy to fly in gusts of up to 38 mph, making it the ideal companion for capturing solo foiling, windsurfing and sailing follow-me footage. $1,299, hoverair.com

Modu Balance Track

Think of this as a jumbo-sized Meccano set, with 17-pieces including four FSC-certified birch wood balance beams (27.6 inches long), four chunky blocks (7.9 x 7.9 x 3.9 inches) made from recycled EPP foam, eight pegs and an idea booklet. Designed for ages from 3 to 8, it’s great for imaginative play, coordination, construction, and problem solving. It’s also surprisingly good value for a kit of this scale. And when the kids finally get bored of balancing, they can be repurposed into a shelving unit. $203, modutoy.com

Timex Time Machines 29mm Dinosaur Watch

Tells time in any era, not just the Jurassic. Made just for kids, Timex's 29mm dinosaur-themed watch boasts an easy-to-read dial, minute markers and adjustable elastic band. The quartz movement means accuracy is assured, while the front glass is actually polymer, so it's not just got good impact resistance, it can be easily polished to remove scuffs should playtime get rowdy. One last boon: all of Timex's kids’ watches come with a 100-percent worry-free replacement plan, so don’t fret about lost or broken watches. $49, timex.com

UNO Canvas x MoMA Card Game

This is the latest in a series of creative collaborations from Mattel Toys, bringing together the world’s best-selling card game and a selection of the most iconic artists from MoMa’s permanent collection. Featuring Sonia Delaunay, Henri Matisse, Piet Mondrian, Claude Monet, Liubov Popova and Vincent van Gogh, it’s a great limited-edition update to the 52-year-old game. And before you ask, sadly the Dutch post-impressionist painter still stacks the +4. $25, mattel.com

Blipblox After Dark

Are you frustrated that your kids don’t ask you enough about your love for The Human League, Cabaret Voltaire, and why Talk Talk’s The Party’s Over is the seminal synth album of 1982? Maybe you can Sparks their imagination with this brilliantly inclusive designed-for-all-ages synth. It comes pre-loaded with 300 built-in melodies and 100 drum sounds, meaning you (sorry, they) can get modulating, pitch-shifting and oscillating straight out the box. The built-in speaker and AA battery power make it easy to use anywhere, but the MIDI input and a quarter-inch output mean it can plug into “proper” gear later. $219, blipblox.com

Dex Camera

Take a photo and Dex identifies what’s in the frame, then teaches the word in one of 16 languages. It can turn pictures into flash cards and use spoken stories to, you know, make learning fun. $249, dex.camera

title: Stalker 2 developer refutes claims by studio founder that Xbox paid more than game's development cost to make it exclusive
author: Sherif Saed
content:
"That is simply not true."

Earlier this week, GSC Game World studio founder Sergiy Grygorovych made a bombshell revelation about the development of Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl. Grygorovych said in an interview with YouTuber OLDboi that Microsoft paid a significant sum to keep the then-upcoming open-world shooter a timed Xbox exclusive.

According to Grygorovych, Microsoft paid the Ukrainian studio more than it cost to develop the game in order to release it on Xbox, and not PlayStation. "It paid for itself before the first day," Grygorovych said, via machine translation.

GSC has now itself responded to those claims, saying they don't paint an accurate picture. In a statement to Insider Gaming, the developer explained that it initially decided to ignore the claims, but felt it must now set the record straight "as continued silence may be perceived as confirmation of information that is simply not true."

"In accordance with the agreements reached between the parties, Sergiy was not involved either in negotiations with partners regarding Stalker 2 or in the actual development of the game throughout its full production cycle," the developer said.

"We have always fully honored these agreements on our side. For this reason, his comments regarding the company's activities cannot be considered an accurate reflection of the actual state of affairs."

Although the statement doesn't specifically counter the claim itself, it does say "the majority of the development budget" was funded by studio owner Max Krippa.

"The development of Stalker 2 became one of the most challenging projects in the history of the video game industry," the statement went on. "We believe the story of this game should be based on facts, not on assumptions or subjective opinions."

In the original interview, Grygorovych said there was a combination of factors that pushed Microsoft to pay for Stalker 2's timed-exclusivity. The tech giant had the cash to spare and, in an effort to score points against Sony, went after Stalker 2. The game's reveal trailer performed really well online, too, according to Grygorovych, which convinced it to make the deal.

"They brought in all the documents for signing in about a week," he said.

Stalker 2 has had a tumultuous development journey, in part due to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The game had to be delayed multiple times, and launched in a rough technical state. It wasn't especially well-received when it initially arrived in late 2024, but GSC has been diligently working on it since, releasing multiple major patches that touched everything from performance to AI routines, animations and more. The game's Xbox timed-exclusivity ended one year later, in November 2025.

title: Less than a month after launching Empulse, it looks like Splitgate dev 1047 Games are laying off more staff
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
It's unclear how many have been affected

Things are sounding bad over at Splitgate developer 1047 Games once again. After launching Empulse last month, a wall-running, quite Titanfall-esque FPS with mechs game that James had some fun with, it appears that layoffs have taken place at the studio, marking the third round of them in the space of about a year.

This comes courtesy of Game Developer, who spotted several developers that have shared looking for work posts on LinkedIn. "As of the end of this week, it will be my last day at 1047 Games due to the third wave of studio layoffs," wrote an associate art director earlier this week. "Throughout the years in this industry, my main goal has always been to work with inspiring artists and art directors, which was a significant reason why I joined. Unfortunately, that didn’t last as long as I hoped, but I’m grateful for the experience and the wonderful people I had the chance to work with."

The studio's community specialist also shared word of being laid off last week, as well as its QA director, who said, "Another new experience for me - drafting a 'part of a layoff' post on LinkedIn. I have seen so many in the last few years, yet I have been lucky enough to not have to post one myself until now. Basing it on my goodbye message to the remainder of the 1047 Games, here it goes. A bunch of us, "the crew" aboard the 1047 train, are getting off on this post-Empulse station. It has been an interesting ride, bumpy at times, narrowly avoiding derailment and with everyone working hard to keep that 1047 train going."

It is unclear how many staffers have been laid off during this latest round. The first time was also an unspecified number, and the second time saw 45 workers losing their jobs. It's also not clear as to why these layoffs have taken place. Empulse generally seems to have been received well, but whether there are enough people playing, especially given it's an early access release, is another question.

title: The FBI has arrested a 21-year-old Florida man alleged to have stolen $220,000 through Steam using malware-ridden games
author: Connor Makar
content:
Law and Order: CPU.

The FBI has arrested a 21-year-old Florida man alleged to have stolen roughly $220,000 of crypto currency using malware installed alongside games. And while the PC platform used to nab this catch isn't explicitly specified, the infested games listed by the FBI were present on Steam until recently.

According to the indictment, the suspect is accused of running this cybercrime operation with several co-conspirators for around two years. During this time, they added malware to eight video games. When downloaded, these would scrape a victim's PC of passwords, which were then used to access cryptocurrency wallets.

According to investigators assigned to this case, these games were promoted on social media by the group, and even used bots to target people identified as owning considerable amounts of crypto. The FBI found the suspect after linking stolen Bitcoin to giftcards, which were used to pay for UberEats for the most part. That's a lot of burgers.

The games used to infect computers with Malware include Lunara, PirateFi, BlockBlasters, and Lampy (the latter was infected with malware after an update). These games were taken off Steam earlier this year, when the FBI announced it was investigating the distribution of malware on the platform.

With an ever-growing number of games released to digital platforms by smaller creators every year, and software such as generative AI being used to create playable games at an astounding rate, one has to wonder if this sort of problem will only become more common in the future. Here's hoping this FBI indictment will dissuade like-minded ne'er-do-wells, while encouraging platform owners like Valve to create the tools needed to stop it.

title: Despite outrage at Sony's shift towards a discless future, only seven PlayStation games have managed more than 100,000 physical sales in the US this year
author: Connor Makar
content:
Boxed in.

Sony's planned shift away from producing physical discs for PlayStation might be unpopular, but new sales data has highlighted the stark business reality behind it.

According to analyst Mat Piscatella from Circana, who references the company's Retail Tracking Service, only two PlayStation video games have managed more than 10,000 physical sales in the US during the week ending on the 11th July.

For a more macro perspective, only seven PlayStation games have sold more than 100,000 physical copies this year-to-date (meaning from the 1st January until today) in the US. While this is focused on one global market, it is one of the largest in the video game industry by revenue spent. As such, consumer trends there have considerable influence.

These statistics were posted in response to outrage online that has been consistently levied at Sony since the company announced its intention to cease physical disc production in January 2028. This vocal campaign has even flooded onto social media posts for developers making games for PlayStation, even those that will come on a disc, such as Insomniac's latest Wolverine, the latest cinematic trailer for which was soaked in snarky comments.

As of writing, Sony has shown no inclination to concede any ground to this uproar. Industry experts have spoken at great lengths about the decision, pointing to both the smart business sense behind this decision, as well as the wider consequences of its implementation to consumer rights and to other valid concerns. All the while, even government superpowers like the European Union seem unable to intercede - Sony is free to sell games in whatever format it likes, for good or for ill.

Even so, the fire behind these complaints from physical video game lovers seems unlikely to die out any time soon. Perhaps an old idiom is relevant here: sometimes you've got to put your money where your mouth is.

title: Asha Sharma-appointed Xbox VP of engineering leaves a mere three months after being moved over from Microsoft's CoreAI team
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Cognitive dissonance.

When Microsoft assigned Asha Sharma as the new leader of the Xbox division in February, replacing the Phil Spencer regime, the executive brought along some of her former colleagues with her. Now, one of those recent hires is leaving.

Jared Palmer, who previously held the title of Xbox VP of engineering, announced on X (via Kotaku) that he's joined Cognition, an AI company. "Personal update: I've joined Cognition to lead engineering," he wrote. "I'm grateful to Asha Sharma and everyone at Xbox for an amazing year."

Palmer was among several of Sharma's former colleagues at Microsoft's CoreAI team, which the executive brought to the Xbox team in May. At the time, she said Palmer will work on developer tools, engineering, product and infrastructure.

"He's spent his career building developer tools that remove friction and increase productivity," Sharma said of Palmer at the time. "That's exactly the mindset we want, using technology to support creators."

Palmer's stint at Microsoft as a whole has been brief, having joined CoreAI in October last year, before moving to the Xbox team seven months later. It's not clear what prompted the VP to leave after such a short period at Xbox, but the reason could have more to do with where he's going rather than anything to do with Microsoft.

Palmer leaves Xbox at the most tumultuous time in its history. As part of Asha Sharma's big reset plan, the executive laid off 1,600 people across almost all of the studios it owns, with further 1,600 to be laid off over the course of fiscal year 2027, for a total of 3,200. As part of the same campaign, Microsoft is divesting itself from four studios it previously owned, and is proposing the closure of another.

It's not clear what effect this is going to have on the future of the platform, particularly when it comes to Xbox's next-gen console Project Helix, as the year or so preceding a new console launch is typically when most of that platform work is concentrated.

title: Following layoffs and muddy strategy shifts, Xbox announces Backward Compatibility on PC program, with Blinx and Conker leading the first wave
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
Past distractions.

As Microsoft tries to downplay the effects on its gaming business of cutting 3,200 jobs and four studios, Xbox is rethinking its whole strategy even if the more recent comments from inside the house still sound confused at best. Don't worry though; old Xbox games are coming to PC.

Via Xbox Wire, the company has announced Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC, a surprise program that aims to bring 'classics' - more on this below - to PC and handhelds like the ROG Xbox Ally for the first time ever. The emulation effort also includes features like "graphics settings, including up to 4x resolution upscaling, VSync support, Fullscreen and Windowed display modes, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, and more."

The first batch of games includes four oldies you may or may not have played before: Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy. Though there are very vocal voices out there when it comes to gassing up games like Crimson Skies, these aren't system sellers. Still, we have to respect the effort, especially at a time when everyone is selling remakes and remasters while making old releases hard to buy and play. Earlier this generation, Xbox's backwards compatibility project was one of the brand's biggest strengths, so it's nice to see it revived and evolved in some way.

According to the announcement, "each of these games is now available for purchase on PC and also included with all Xbox Game Pass plans", with the separate purchase prices sitting at $9.99 (regional prices may vary). "If you already own a digital license for these games on console, that license now carries over to your PC or handheld," so that's also neat. They have cloud support, too.

"We plan to add even more features to Xbox Backward Compatibility games in the future," Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox, teased. In fact, these first four games will get achievements in the coming months. The sudden and half-baked nature of this first wave makes me think that, even if the push is well-meaning, this is another "break in case of emergency" fast reveal, like last week's Bethesda roadmap.

It's unclear if this move signals a return to the backwards compatibility efforts for Xbox consoles as well, but it's certainly a step in the right direction. Elsewhere, it's unclear if Sony's PlayStation 6 will even have a disc drive to play games from previous generations after it was revealed the company would drop physical game releases entirely starting in 2028. Platforms like GOG are still trying to fight to preserve all sorts of games, though.

title: Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 confirms release date and it's closer than you think
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Planet now.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 will release on 25th August 2026.

Details of an unannounced Aliens: Fireteam Elite sequel popped up as early as July 2024, when a pitch deck detailing "a new chapter in the Aliens: Fireteam Elite" series leaked online. At that time, it was expected to launch by Q3 2025.

Then, in May, the game was finally confirmed, only this time with a release window of Q3 2026 instead.

In an extraordinarily brief, action-packed, and thoroughly gore-soaked teaser, Cold Iron revealed the release date and teased "new perks, abilities, weapons, Xenomorphs, and more".

ICYMI, the sequel expands from three-player co-op to four players, as well as "deeper strategies and smoother coordination with your squad, [with] a variety of new classes and weapons each bringing unique playstyles and tactical possibilities to the battlefield".

Other features include an updated horde mode, a new Specialist endgame class for fully custom Marines, five unique classes, and "deadlier threats". Players will also be able to team up cross-platform with in-game voice chat. It's coming to PC via Steam and Epic Games Store, as well as the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

"Aliens: Fireteam Elite is exactly what it says on the tin. Stuffed with guns, gadgets, and plentiful alien goo, it's a frenetic cooperative firefight against some of sci-fi's most iconic monsters in an all-new tale that takes us beyond the original trilogy," I wrote when I reviewed Aliens: Fireteam Elite back in 2021.

"No, it's not the most sophisticated shooter, and no, its truncated runtime is unlikely to occupy you for more than a couple of nights, but it's an unashamedly good romp that'll hopefully satisfy your Ripley power fantasies, too."

title: What are we all playing this weekend?
author: James Archer
content:
Well? Do tell!

I spent most of last Saturday laid out in a Baku hotel room, muscles in both legs ground to flecks of useless meat by the decision to walk down a mountain when there was a perfectly good funicular right there. May this weekend be more fruitful, and less marred by the stupidity of trying to please a step counter that only truly cares about where its next battery charge is coming from. Ruinous silicone bastard.

Edwin: After writing about Star Wars: Zero Company this week I feel a hankering for a tactics RPG of some kind. Perhaps I'll dig out that Troubleshooter: Abandoned Children game you're all so keen on, or maybe I will fire up Othercide on the Switch (assuming the interface, which I recall being torturous on PS4, transfers easily to the smaller screen). Beyond that, I've just bought a new poetry tome, Aaron Kent's Angels the Size of Houses.

Jeremy: This weekend I'll either be chugging along with Black Flag Resynced or maybe returning to Lords of the Fallen, which got put on the backburner after I decided to be a pirate for a bit rather than an emo goth knight wandering through a depressing world where everything's gone to shite. Speaking of post-apocalyptic worlds, there's also another secret game along these lines that I'll be firing up for guides prep sometime soon. Look to the release schedule in August for possible hints, I say!

James: I slapped Replaced on my Steam Deck last week for the pre-muscledeath plane trip, then spent the whole flight in Silksong instead. What can I say, I can’t get enough bug gibberish. I should play Replaced more, though.

Ollie: Sorry, the bargo gods hath sewn shut my mouth.

Mark: I've been thinking I might finally get around to trying Assassin's Creed Rogue. It's the entry that followed on from the recently resynced Black Flag and attempted to build on the naval battles I loved in that game, but I've never gotten around to giving it a go. It's not unique in that regard, I've missed a number of AC entries in the years since Black Flag, specifically Valhalla, Origins and Syndicate. I should also really get around to finishing the remastered version of Assassin's Creed 3 after starting it about half a decade ago. God, there are just so many games about people in hoodies jumping around.

Julian, Dion, and Callum do not recognise the the weekend's claim to the end of the week.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend?...

title: Trump Plans to Impose New Illegal Tariffs on Canada
author: IlyaSomin
content:
Today, Donald Trump announced plans to impose 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian imports to the United States:

President Trump is imposing 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, from hockey equipment to alcoholic beverages, escalating the trade dispute between the two countries.

The new tariffs — laid out in a series of proclamations signed by Mr. Trump on Monday — are set to take effect on Aug. 19. The White House accused Canada of "unreasonable, unequal, and discriminatory actions" by imposing tariffs or import restrictions on certain American goods, some of which began after Mr. Trump's initial round of tariffs on Canada last year.

In retaliation for last year's Canadian tariffs on certain U.S. auto imports, the Trump administration slapped tariffs on certain Canadian electronics, hockey equipment, honey, flower bulbs, down feathers, plywood, cowhides, jewelry and other goods. The White House also imposed tariffs on Canadian beer, wine, liquor and milk, in response to Canadian boycotts of U.S. alcohol in response to last year's tariffs and longstanding Canadian quotas on dairy imports.

Goods that flow across the border under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA — a trade deal inked during Mr. Trump's first term — will not be exempt from the new tariffs, a senior administration official told reporters Monday.

The new tariffs are based on Section 338 of the notorious 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff legislation, which severely exacerbated the Great Depression. As Philip Zelikow of the conservative Hoover Institution explained in a guest post here at the VC blog, last year, Section 338 was long-ago superseded by new legislation enacted in 1962 and 1974, and is therefore defunct. For that reason, it has not been used since at least the 1940s.

Georgetown University trade policy scholar Peter Harrell summarizes additional useful points about the new tariffs on Twitter, including some additional legal objections to them. Should the new tariffs come into effect, there will likely be legal challenges, and those challenges will richly deserve to prevail.

I would add that this is just the latest of a series of efforts by Trump to usurp congressional tariff authority and impose harmful and dangerous trade restrictions that damage the US economy and poison relations with our allies and trading partners, of which Canada is one of the most important. That includes the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court in February, in a case I helped bring, the  Section 122 tariffs  invalidated by the US Court of International Trade, his massive planned Section 301 tariffs, and - most recently - his threat to impose tariffs on Canada in response to wildfires there. Courts should continue to reject these dangerous power grabs and affronts to the rule of law.

I may well have more to say about these new tariffs later, especially if they end up getting implemented, as currently planned.
